title: Review of the "Misalignment in high-stakes settings" section in Anthropic's Risk Report (August 2026)
summary: Scope and access: this review was written based solely on Anthropic’s internal Risk Report from August 2026 and is relatively lightweight. The authors of this review were engaged prior to the “ An update on independent evaluators ” announcement and did not have the level of access to information described in that post. We expect future engagements to be governed by different terms. Redaction summary statement: Anthropic had the right to veto publication of this review and to redact any part of it. No redactions were made to our review and we did not change any of our conclusions during the publication review process. METR made minor changes to our review in response to feedback from Anthropic, but these changes were limited to minor wording and clarification, as well as improving the methodology of an experiment we ran. Executive summary METR conducted an external review of the “Misalignment in high-stakes settings” section of Anthropic’s Risk Report: August 2026 . Anthropic’s report concludes that, as of July 15, 2026, “the risk of catastrophic harm caused by misalignment of [their] models is low.” Our best guess is that we agree with Anthropic that the risk of catastrophic harm from misalignment is low for the models covered in the report. However, this is primarily due to models’ limited capabilities, rather than safeguards and alignment training. title: GLM-5.3 Sometimes Considers How Train-Time Actions Shape Future Behavior
summary: Authors: Axel Højmark*, Ezra Newman* (*Equal contribution) While reviewing transcripts from standard behavioral evaluations of GLM-5.3, we noticed that the model occasionally reasons, unprompted, about how its actions will shape future models. It appears to consider that its outputs might be used for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), or other forms of training, and that the actions it takes could reinforce certain behaviors. For example, GLM-5.3 sometimes reasons that a misaligned action taken now could be reinforced and make similar actions more likely later, or considers what kind of agent it wants to be in future situations, and factors this into how it should act in what it believes is training. We refer to this general reasoning pattern as update-aware reasoning : the model reasons about how its actions will influence training updates or behavior beyond the current episode. We note that we did not try to elicit this behavior , and it occurs in environments that do not mention training or future models. Update-aware reasoning is concerning because it is a key capability and propensity that underpins alignment faking : a misaligned model could strategically behave aligned during training so that training does not change its goals, and then pursue those goals once it is no longer being trained (in deployment). title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
summary: Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API 1 . These models promise fast, inexpensive classification. Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges 2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case. We’ve also noticed people using the default decision threshold of 0.50 without checking whether it works well for their task. This can leave a lot of performance on the table. In this post, we’ll start by showing how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models. With those thresholds tuned, we’ll compare cost and performance to help you assess which model fits your use case. Finally, we’ll explore how to interpret model scores when deciding whether to act, and how calibration can make them more useful as confidence estimates. What we tested We used 100 traces, or logs of conversations and actions, from an apartment leasing agent. The task is to identify traces containing an error, such as a failed booking or a missed handoff to a human. 3 We used the same dataset and broad failure-finding task in our prior post on automated evals . title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
summary: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other.
